planting.note: Root short stem cuttings or divide rooted sections in warm, humid conditions in spring; this species is noticeably more cold-tolerant than most tropical peperomias and can summer outdoors in deep shade in milder zones.

directions: Grow in dense shade in humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil or potting mix, mimicking the shaded rocky slopes and forest floors of Japan, Taiwan, and Korea where this species grows wild. It forms a low, creeping mat of small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves on thin trailing stems, spreading slowly by rooting at the nodes to make a fine-textured groundcover for shaded rock gardens in mild climates or a houseplant/terrarium subject elsewhere. Unlike the thicker-leaved tropical peperomias in cultivation, it prefers steadier moisture and will not tolerate prolonged drying between waterings. Trim back lightly to keep the mat dense and propagate easily from any rooted stem section.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in a light, fast-draining mix under warm, humid conditions; keep out of direct sun while new roots establish.

directions: Grow in bright shade to partial shade in a light, well-aerated potting mix that dries slightly between waterings. Native to the Caribbean and parts of Central America, this trailing species carries small, somewhat fleshy, pointed leaves in opposite pairs along thin wiry stems, giving a delicate, lacy texture distinct from the broader-leaved caperata and obtusifolia types already common in cultivation. It works well cascading from a small hanging pot, tucked into a shaded dish garden, or massed as terrarium understory planting. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage branching and a fuller habit.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Peperomia species

planting.note: Root single-node or short-tip cuttings in a light, moisture-retentive mix under warm, humid conditions; new plants fill in quickly once rooted.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to full shade in a light, well-draining mix kept evenly moist but never soggy. This Brazilian trailing species, increasingly sold in the houseplant trade under names like Isabela, bears tiny rounded leaves covered in fine short hairs along slender reddish stems, giving the foliage a soft, slightly fuzzy texture that sets it apart from the smooth, marbled leaves of String of Turtles (Peperomia prostrata). It cascades readily from hanging pots or spreads as a low terrarium groundcover, rooting wherever a stem touches moist substrate. Trim back leggy growth periodically to keep the trailing stems dense and well-furnished with foliage.

planting.note: Press short stem pieces directly onto moist terrarium substrate or rooting mix; cuttings root readily at the nodes within one to two weeks under warm, humid conditions.

directions: Grow in medium to low indirect light in a consistently moist, humus-rich substrate, as this Central American species is adapted to damp, shaded forest floors. It forms an extremely fine, mat-forming carpet of tiny rounded leaves on thread-thin creeping stems, finer and lower-growing than the related Pilea depressa and Pilea nummulariifolia already in cultivation, making it a favorite living-groundcover choice for closed terrariums and vivariums. It spreads quickly by rooting along any stem segment that contacts moist substrate, so trim regularly to prevent it from smothering slower-growing companions. Keep humidity high, since the thin leaves wilt quickly if allowed to dry out.

planting.note: Mount on bark or pot loosely in a coarse, fast-draining bark/sphagnum mix in deep shade with high humidity; unlike thin-leaved atmospheric tillandsias, this species wants a central water-holding cup kept topped up rather than a quick dunk-and-dry routine.

directions: Grow in deep, bright shade under high, constant humidity, replicating the cloud-forest understory of Mexico and Central America where this tank-forming bromeliad grows as an epiphyte on tree trunks and branches. It forms a substantial rosette of broad, strap-shaped leaves cupped tightly at the base to hold a reservoir of water and debris, a very different growth form from the wiry, silver-scaled, moisture-shedding air plants that dominate the rest of the genus in cultivation. In maturity it sends up a dramatic bract of rose-pink to red coloring from which tubular violet flowers emerge, a showy event after what is otherwise a slow-growing, long-lived foliage plant. Keep the central cup filled with water (flushing it periodically to prevent stagnation) and never let this species dry out the way xeric Tillandsia species tolerate.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Tillandsia species
